- Protect the skin (swollen skin breaks down easily) and watch for hypertensive encephalopathy, heart failure and renal failure.
- Rest during the active phase, then increase activity as blood and protein in the urine clear.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
Diuretics, antihypertensives and corticosteroids; penicillin if streptococcal infection is still suspected (nephritic). ACE inhibitors, diuretics and lipid-lowering agents (nephrotic).

## Complications and red flags
Headache with high blood pressure and confusion (hypertensive encephalopathy), crackles with neck vein distension (heart failure), falling urine output with rising creatinine (renal failure); in nephrotic, sudden chest pain, breathlessness or a swollen painful leg (clot).

## How the exam asks about it
Match the sign to the disease: eyes puffy plus cola-colored urine after a sore throat is nephritic; whole-body swelling with heavy protein loss is nephrotic. The question often asks which finding needs action first: respiratory distress or high blood pressure with neurologic change beats edema.

## How to reason about it
Inflamed filter -> less filtrate, retained salt and water -> edema, hypertension, hematuria. Leaky filter -> protein loss, fluid leaves vessels -> anasarca. The trap: both diets restrict sodium and protein in this handout, so do not pick the answer that gives a high-protein diet.

## Related topics
[[Acute Glomerulonephritis (Nephritic Syndrome)]], [[Nephrotic Syndrome]], [[Fluid Volume Excess (Hypervolemia)]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout lists the same nursing care for both diseases and says "erythropoietin sedimentation rate" (it means erythrocyte sedimentation rate). Protein restriction in nephrotic syndrome is debated; confirm. Hematuria is more typical of nephritic than nephrotic, so treat "rest until hematuria resolves" under nephrotic as copied text.

title: Cystitis, Urethritis and Pyelonephritis Compared
body:
## What it is
Three infections of the urinary tract at different levels: the urethra (urethritis), the bladder (cystitis) and the kidney itself (pyelonephritis). Most are caused by bacteria climbing up from the outside, E. coli being the usual culprit.

## Must-know facts
- Cystitis: infection of the bladder, usually an ascending infection through the urethra. More common in women because the urethra is short, close to the rectum, and affected by childbirth and estrogen changes; sexual intercourse also raises the risk. In men it follows epididymitis, prostatitis or stones.
- Urethritis: inflammation of the urethra by E. coli, staphylococci, streptococci or Pseudomonas; it looks like gonorrheal urethritis but is not caused by sexual contact. It can lead to prostatitis and epididymitis. Burning on urination and pus-like discharge appearing 3-14 days after exposure.
- Pyelonephritis: infection of the kidney. Acute form comes from instrumentation of the urethra or spread through the blood. Chronic form is linked to obstruction or backflow (stone, tumor, neurogenic bladder) and slowly scars the kidney, causing weight loss, hypertension and renal failure.
- Lower tract signs: dysuria, urgency, frequency, nocturia, suprapubic pain, pyuria, hematuria. Upper tract (kidney) signs add fever, chills, flank pain, costovertebral tenderness and malaise.
- Chronic pyelonephritis: fatigue, headache, poor appetite, polyuria, thirst and weight loss.

## Assessment
Urinalysis and urine culture and sensitivity (positive for E. coli in cystitis). Cystoscopy, IVP, ultrasound and CT scan are used for pyelonephritis to look for an obstruction.

## Priority nursing actions
- Obtain the culture specimen before starting antibiotics, so the organism can still be grown.
- Give antibiotics on time and finish the course; give antispasmodics and analgesics for comfort.
- Push fluids (handout: 3-4 L/day for pyelonephritis) unless restricted; cranberry or orange juice; avoid coffee, tea and alcohol that irritate the bladder.
- Pyelonephritis: complete bed rest, vital signs, intake and output and weight.
- Teach front-to-back perineal hygiene, frequent voiding and emptying the bladder after intercourse.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
Antibiotics (the handout names co-trimoxazole as drug of choice for cystitis, and tetracycline or doxycycline for urethritis), antispasmodics, analgesics; warm sitz bath for cystitis comfort.

## Complications and red flags
Fever with chills and flank pain suggests the infection has reached the kidney; fever, low blood pressure and confusion suggest sepsis; urinary retention is both a cause and a complication.

## How the exam asks about it
Which sign tells you the infection is in the kidney rather than the bladder? Flank pain, costovertebral tenderness, fever and chills. Which teaching prevents recurrence? Fluids, wiping front to back, voiding after sex.

## How to reason about it
Ascending infection -> bladder -> kidney. The trap: a client whose symptoms stop early may stop antibiotics; the nurse stresses completing the course.

## Related topics
[[Cystitis and Urethritis]], [[Pyelonephritis]], [[Urolithiasis: Kidney and Urinary Stones]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout lists "pain in the flank area" under cystitis, which usually points to the kidney; check. Choice of antibiotic and doses must come from your pharmacology text.

title: Peritoneal Dialysis versus Hemodialysis Compared
body:
## What it is
Dialysis does the filtering job of failed kidneys: it removes waste, extra fluid and excess electrolytes. Peritoneal dialysis (PD) uses the client's own peritoneal membrane inside the belly. Hemodialysis (HD) pushes the blood through a machine with an artificial membrane.

## Must-know facts
- Both rely on diffusion and osmosis; hemodialysis also uses ultrafiltration to pull off fluid.
- PD: dialysate runs through a catheter into the peritoneal cavity; the peritoneum, which lines the abdominal wall and covers organs, is the semipermeable membrane. The client can dialyze alone, in any location, and PD can be used even when the blood pressure is unstable.
- HD: blood travels from the client, through a membrane bathed in dialysate, and back, using an arteriovenous (AV) fistula, an AV graft, or a large double-lumen catheter placed in the subclavian, internal jugular or femoral vein.
- AV fistula: artery joined to vein, often in the forearm; takes at least 14 days to mature. Graft: used when the client's vessels are not suitable for a fistula. Catheter: temporary, higher infection risk.
- PD drainage: normally colorless; cloudy means infection or peritonitis; bloody is acceptable in the first few exchanges; yellowish suggests a punctured bladder.

## Assessment
- PD: baseline vital signs and weight, abdominal pain, drainage color and volume, catheter site, and signs of peritonitis (fever, cloudy fluid, belly pain).
- HD: feel for the thrill and listen for the bruit over the access every time; check the limb for color, warmth and sensation; weight and blood pressure before and after.

## Priority nursing actions
- PD preparation: consent, baseline vital signs, explain the procedure, empty bladder and bowel (to prevent puncture), warm the dialysate (warming dilates the peritoneal vessels), regulate inflow and outflow, and use strict asepsis because infection is the main risk.
- HD access care: protect the access; absence of bruit or thrill means blockage or clotting and is reported at once. No blood pressures, needle sticks or tight items on the access arm.
- Give antihypertensives only as directed, since the handout says hold them before dialysis to avoid blood pressure falling too low.
- Catheter site care at showering; do not soak the exit site; keep the catheter secured.
- Itching: antihistamines, bath oils, lotion, trimmed nails.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
Heparin may be added to prevent fibrin in PD; antibiotics may be given by the PD route per orders.

## Complications and red flags
PD: leaks, outflow obstruction, peritonitis, exit-site infection, high glucose. HD: poor flow, clotting, infection, aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm, hand ischemia, heart failure from the extra blood flow.

## How the exam asks about it
Cloudy PD return = peritonitis. No bruit over a fistula = clot, call the physician. Unstable blood pressure favors PD.

## How to reason about it
Protect the lifeline first (access or catheter), watch for infection, then think comfort. The trap: do not use the fistula arm for blood pressure or IV.

## Related topics
[[Peritoneal Dialysis]], [[Hemodialysis and Vascular Access]], [[Chronic Kidney Disease: Diet and Nursing Care]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout lists "monitor urine/glucose levels" and "antibiotic prophylaxis" for PD; the usual practice and the PD antibiotic route are textbook content. The handout says antihypertensives "must be withheld" before dialysis; confirm with your textbook and unit policy.

title: Acute Kidney Injury: Prerenal, Intrarenal and Postrenal Causes
body:
## What it is
Acute renal failure (also called acute kidney injury) is a sudden drop or stop in kidney function that is often reversible. The wastes (urea, creatinine) pile up. Sorting the cause by location tells you what to treat.

## Must-know facts
- Prerenal: the kidney is starved of blood flow although the kidney tissue itself is healthy. Causes in the handout: volume depletion, weak heart, vasodilation.
- Intrarenal (intrinsic): the kidney tissue is damaged. Causes: prolonged ischemia (acute tubular necrosis), nephrotoxic drugs or substances, infection or inflammation.
- Postrenal: urine cannot leave. Causes: obstruction of the urinary tract by stones, tumors, benign prostatic hyperplasia, or blood clots.
- Course in four phases: onset (1-3 days), oliguric (urine below 400 mL/24 h, lasting 3 days to 2 weeks), diuretic (urine 3-5 L/day), recovery (3-12 months).
- Oliguric labs: high BUN and creatinine, high potassium, low sodium, high phosphate, low calcium, metabolic acidosis, azotemia, proteinuria, casts, red and white cells in the urine.

## Assessment
Sudden fall in urine output, edema, high blood pressure, headache, irritability, tingling, restlessness, twitching or convulsions, pallor, ammonia breath odor, drowsiness progressing to coma. Check intake and output hourly if instructed.

## Priority nursing actions
- Find the cause: a prerenal problem is fixed with volume or cardiac support; a postrenal one is fixed by relieving the obstruction (a catheter may be needed); an intrarenal one needs removal of the toxin and support.
- Monitor potassium and ECG because hyperkalemia is the most dangerous early problem; protect against fluid overload (daily weight, lung sounds, neck veins).
- During the diuretic phase, watch for dehydration and low potassium because lots of urine is passed even though wastes are still high.
- Avoid nephrotoxic drugs; give skin care, rest, and protect from injury; prepare for dialysis if needed.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
Treat the cause; dopamine to improve kidney blood flow, loop diuretics, ACE inhibitors for blood pressure, H2 blockers to prevent ulcers, Kayexalate for potassium, sodium bicarbonate for acidosis; moderate protein restriction, high carbohydrate and limited potassium; sometimes parenteral nutrition.

## Complications and red flags
Dysrhythmias from potassium, pulmonary edema and heart failure, seizures, sepsis, progression to chronic renal failure.

## How the exam asks about it
Matching: dehydration or shock = prerenal; aminoglycoside or contrast injury = intrarenal; enlarged prostate or stone = postrenal. Priority question: what do you watch during oliguria? Potassium and fluid status.

## How to reason about it
Before the kidney (low flow) -> in the kidney (damage) -> after the kidney (blockage). The trap: urine output rising in the diuretic phase does not mean the kidney is fully healed.

## Related topics
[[Acute Renal Failure: Causes, Phases and Findings]], [[Acute Renal Failure: Treatment and Nursing Care]], [[Hyperkalemia]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's "volume expanders (dopamine)" is imprecise; dopamine is not a volume expander. Confirm all drug uses and the diuretic-phase hypokalemia detail in a pharmacology text. Cause examples such as aminoglycosides and contrast dye are added by me.

title: Medicines Used in Kidney and Urinary Disorders
body:
## What it is
A quick list of the drug groups the handout names for kidney and urinary problems, with the reason for each. Doses are not given here; use your drug reference.

## Must-know facts
- Co-trimoxazole: drug of choice for cystitis (urinary infection). Tetracycline or doxycycline: urethritis.
- Antispasmodics and analgesics: bladder spasm and pain in infections and stones; narcotic analgesics for stone colic.
- Allopurinol: lowers uric acid in uric acid stones.
- Terazosin: alpha-1 blocker that relaxes the bladder sphincter in benign prostatic hyperplasia. Finasteride: blocks 5-alpha reductase so the prostate shrinks.
- Penicillin: when streptococcal infection may remain in glomerulonephritis. Corticosteroids, diuretics and antihypertensives also used.
- ACE inhibitors and lipid-lowering agents: nephrotic syndrome; ACE inhibitors also for kidney-failure hypertension.
- Dopamine: improves kidney blood flow in acute failure. Loop diuretics: increase urine. H2 blockers: prevent stress ulcers.
- Kayexalate: removes potassium. Sodium bicarbonate: treats acidosis.
- Calcium and phosphorus binders (for example aluminum hydroxide gel, Amphojel): lower phosphate in kidney failure and phosphate stones.
- Erythropoietin: treats anemia of kidney failure and replaces blood transfusion before a transplant.
- Antiseizure agents and antihypertensives: complications of uremia.
- Immunosuppressants: prevent rejection after kidney transplant.
- Diuretics for fluid overload: thiazides block sodium reabsorption in the distal tubule; loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide) work in the loop of Henle; spironolactone acts in the last part of the distal tubule and can raise potassium.

## Priority nursing actions
- Before giving a drug, ask what it will change and what lab or vital sign you must check first (potassium for diuretics and Kayexalate, blood pressure for antihypertensives, hearing and kidney function for gentamicin).
- Avoid nephrotoxic drugs in kidney failure; tell clients to avoid aspirin and over-the-counter products containing sodium or magnesium.

## Complications and red flags
Hypokalemia with potassium-wasting diuretics, hyperkalemia with spironolactone and in kidney failure, hypotension with alpha blockers, infection with immunosuppressants.

## Client teaching
Take antibiotics as prescribed, rise slowly with alpha blockers, report weight gain or swelling, never self-medicate with over-the-counter drugs in kidney disease.

## How the exam asks about it
Match drug to disease: finasteride and terazosin = prostate; allopurinol = uric acid stones; Kayexalate = high potassium; erythropoietin = renal anemia.

## Related topics
[[Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)]], [[Hyperkalemia]], [[Chronic Kidney Disease: Diet and Nursing Care]]

## Check against your textbook
Antibiotic choices change with local resistance; verify all drug uses and side effects. The handout's "volume expanders (Dopamine)" is imprecise.

title: Electrolyte Effects on ECG, Nerves and Muscles
body:
## What it is
Potassium, calcium, magnesium, sodium and phosphate all control how nerves and muscles fire, so imbalances show up in the heart tracing and in muscle behavior. This note pulls those findings into one place.

## Must-know facts
- Low potassium (hypokalemia): prominent U wave and flat T wave, irregular rhythm, muscle weakness, paralysis, irritability, high blood sugar, rhabdomyolysis, and dilute urine with polyuria in long-standing cases.
- High potassium (hyperkalemia): peaked narrow T waves, longer PR interval, shortened QT progressing to a widened QRS, and then ventricular fibrillation; tingling, weakness, constipation, lethargy.
- Low calcium: prolonged QT; excitable nerves with cramps, tetany, laryngospasm, Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs.
- High calcium: shortened QT; slowed nerves with anorexia, nausea, vomiting, weakness, drowsiness, coma.
- Low magnesium: neuromuscular weakness, irritability, convulsions, tetany, ECG changes. High magnesium: low blood pressure, weakness, trouble breathing, irregular heartbeat, mental changes.
- Phosphate: low levels weaken breathing and heart muscle; high levels cause low calcium findings (tetany, Chvostek, Trousseau) and a prolonged QT.
- Sodium: low sodium causes headache, confusion and seizure; high sodium causes thirst, twitching and delirium.

## Assessment
Look at the pattern: too little of an excitable ion (calcium, magnesium) gives twitching and cramps, while too much slows everything down. For potassium, both directions affect the heart rhythm, so any abnormal potassium level needs a heart check.

## Priority nursing actions
- Heart rhythm and breathing first: connect cardiac monitoring in significant potassium, calcium or magnesium imbalance; keep airway equipment ready for laryngospasm.
- Check which level is abnormal before reaching for a treatment; replace or lower according to the order.
- Seizure precautions for low calcium, low magnesium, low sodium and high phosphate.

## Complications and red flags
Ventricular fibrillation (high potassium), cardiac arrest, laryngospasm and seizure (low calcium), respiratory arrest (high magnesium).

## How the exam asks about it
Given an ECG description, name the electrolyte: peaked T = high potassium, U wave = low potassium, long QT = low calcium, short QT = high calcium. Then give the priority action.

## How to reason about it
Which ion is off -> how does it change the nerve or muscle -> what is the most dangerous organ effect (the heart or the airway)? The trap: do not give potassium fast or without checking kidney function and urine output.

## Related topics
[[Hypokalemia]], [[Hyperkalemia]], [[Hypocalcemia]], [[Hypercalcemia]], [[Magnesium Imbalances]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout lists "shortened QT interval" in hyperkalemia and the calcium ECG changes; confirm waveform details in a cardiac text.

title: Electrolyte Partners and Shifts Between Cells and Blood
body:
## What it is
Electrolytes do not change one at a time. Acid-base shifts, hormone levels, protein binding and kidney function link them. The exam often tests these links.

## Must-know facts
- Calcium and phosphate are mirror images: high phosphate = low calcium; low phosphate = high calcium.
- Acidosis pushes hydrogen into cells and potassium out into the blood, so metabolic and respiratory acidosis tend to raise potassium. When acidosis is corrected, potassium moves back and the level can fall, causing hypokalemia.
- Alkalosis pulls hydrogen out of cells in exchange for potassium coming in, so alkalosis, including respiratory alkalosis, lowers potassium. Alkalosis also makes calcium bind to protein, leading to low ionized calcium and tetany.
- Low magnesium and low potassium often go together (low magnesium drives potassium into cells), and low magnesium also lowers calcium.
- Loss of stomach acid (vomiting, NG suction) loses chloride and hydrogen, so metabolic alkalosis comes with low chloride and low potassium.
- Kidney failure raises potassium, phosphate and magnesium and lowers calcium; hence phosphate binders and calcium and vitamin D handling in CKD.
- Aldosterone keeps sodium and loses potassium; "where sodium goes, water follows."
- Hemolyzed blood or cell injury (trauma, rhabdomyolysis) releases potassium and phosphate into the blood.

## Assessment
Always read the ABG together with the electrolytes. A client with diabetic ketoacidosis may have a high serum potassium that hides a body-wide shortage.

## Priority nursing actions
- Ask: what is the pH? Then predict the potassium and calcium changes and check the ECG.
- Monitor potassium closely during insulin and bicarbonate therapy because it falls as acidosis improves.
- In kidney failure, avoid magnesium-containing antacids and phosphorus-rich foods and give binders with meals as ordered.

## Complications and red flags
Dysrhythmias from potassium shifts, tetany from low calcium, respiratory depression from magnesium excess.

## How the exam asks about it
"A client with metabolic acidosis is treated and potassium falls; why?" (potassium returns into the cells). "A client who is hyperventilating has tingling and cramps" (alkalosis lowers ionized calcium).

## How to reason about it
Acid -> potassium up. Base -> potassium down and calcium down. The trap: a normal potassium during acidosis does not mean the body has enough.

## Related topics
[[Hyperkalemia]], [[Hypocalcemia]], [[Phosphate Imbalances]], [[Metabolic Acidosis]]

## Check against your textbook
The binding of calcium to protein in alkalosis is in the handout under hypocalcemia, but the other pairings (magnesium and potassium, DKA masking) are general teaching added by me. Verify details in your fluids and electrolytes text.

title: Burn Phases Compared: Fluids, Labs and Goals
body:
## What it is
A side-by-side view of what the body and the nurse are doing in the three burn phases, so the lab and fluid pattern can be recognized quickly.

## Must-know facts
- Emergent (resuscitative): from injury to completed fluid resuscitation, around the first 24-48 hours. Fluid leaks from vessels into tissue (third spacing), so blood volume falls. Findings: hypotension, fast pulse, oliguria, thirst. Labs: high potassium (cells burst and leak), low sodium, high hematocrit from hemoconcentration, metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss. Goal: prevent hypovolemic shock and keep vital organs working.
- Acute (immediate, diuretic): starts when the client is stable and diuresis begins, about 2-5 days after injury, and ends when the wound is closed. Fluid returns to the vessels. Findings: diuresis, low hematocrit (dilution), high blood pressure, more urine. Labs: low potassium (potassium moves back into cells), low sodium, metabolic acidosis. Goal: close the wound, prevent complications; focus on infection control, wound care, nutrition, pain, physical therapy.
- Rehabilitative (convalescent): from wound closure until the best possible function, which continues after discharge. Goals: independence and maximum function; prevent scars and contractures; rehabilitation, reconstruction and counseling. A full-thickness burn changes from waxy white to dark brown; partial-thickness drying replaces weeping.
- Fluid choice: crystalloid (lactated Ringer's) at first, colloid on the second day.

## Assessment
Hourly urine output is the most sensitive guide to perfusion in the first phase. A urine output above the target or falling hemoglobin and hematocrit may allow the IV rate to be reduced.

## Priority nursing actions
- Emergent: airway, breathing and circulation, then stop the burning process, cool, cover, start IV fluids, transport.
- Acute: prevent infection and give wound care; protect against overload as fluid returns to the vessels; support nutrition.
- Rehabilitative: positioning, splints, exercise and emotional support.

## Complications and red flags
Hypovolemic shock and airway swelling early; fluid overload, infection and sepsis in the acute phase; contractures and psychological stress later.

## How the exam asks about it
Potassium is high early and low in the diuretic phase; hematocrit is high early and low later. The question will often give a lab pattern and ask for the phase.

## How to reason about it
Third spacing -> concentrated blood, low volume, leaking potassium. Mobilization -> diluted blood, high urine volume, potassium back in cells. The trap: a rising urine output after the first day means fluid mobilization, not that resuscitation can stop being watched.

## Related topics
[[Burn Care Phases and Emergency Priorities]], [[Burn Fluid Resuscitation: Parkland and Brooke Formulas]], [[Burn Pathophysiology and Whole-Body Response]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout lists hyponatremia in both emergent and acute phases. Also confirm the day on which colloid is started and the target urine output, taken from the handout's 30-50 mL/hr.

title: Kidney Stone Types and Matching Diets
body:
## What it is
Stones form from different chemicals, so the diet is matched to the stone. The handout divides them by whether they form in acidic or alkaline urine.

## Must-know facts
- Acidic stones: calcium oxalate (foods high in oxalate, such as cabbage, beans, spinach, cranberry, nuts, tea, chocolate), uric acid (anchovies, organ meats, whole grain, nuts, sardines) and cystine (meat, milk, eggs, cheese).
- Alkaline stones: calcium phosphate (dairy products, meat; immobility, obesity, hyperparathyroidism) and struvite (urea-splitting bacteria, linked to infection).
- Acidic stones: alkaline-ash diet (fruits, vegetables, milk). Alkaline stones: acid-ash diet (cranberry, prune, plum, meat and poultry).
- Calcium stone: lower calcium, acid-ash diet, less protein and sodium. Uric acid: low-purine foods, alkaline-ash. Cystine: low methionine, alkaline-ash. Phosphate stone: aluminum hydroxide gel and low phosphorus.
- Fluids: about 3 L/day to help pass the stone.

## Assessment
Renal colic: sudden, severe wave-like pain moving toward the groin and thigh, nausea, vomiting, hematuria, urgency with little urine. Tests: KUB x-ray, IVP, ultrasound, cystoscopy, stone analysis, urinalysis.

## Priority nursing actions
- Pain relief first (analgesics, warm sitz bath, warm compress to the flank).
- Strain every urine specimen through gauze and save any solid material for analysis, because knowing the stone type decides the diet.
- Measure intake and output, encourage fluids and walking.
- Report fever, obstruction or little urine, which suggest infection or blockage.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
Narcotic analgesics, antispasmodics, allopurinol for uric acid, diuretics, antibiotics. Surgery is named by site: nephrolithotomy (kidney), pyelolithotomy (renal pelvis), ureterolithotomy (ureter), cystolithotomy (bladder).

## Complications and red flags
Obstruction, infection and sepsis, hydronephrosis, uncontrolled pain.

## Client teaching
Drink plenty of fluids all day and night, follow the diet for your stone type, and limit foods that carry the offending chemical.

## How the exam asks about it
Match the stone to the diet. A client with uric acid stone should avoid organ meats and sardines.

## How to reason about it
Acidic stone -> make urine alkaline; alkaline stone -> make urine acidic. The trap: do not give the "acid-ash" diet to a client whose stone forms in acid urine.

## Related topics
[[Urolithiasis: Kidney and Urinary Stones]], [[Pyelonephritis]], [[Cystitis and Urethritis]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout lists cranberry under both oxalate-rich foods and acid-ash foods, and places calcium oxalate diets with other advice; check. The handout's "calcium stone: low calcium diet" is simplified; modern teaching varies.

title: Urine and Blood Findings Across Kidney Disorders
body:
## What it is
A summary of which urine and blood results to expect in each kidney or fluid problem, so the lab pattern can lead you to the diagnosis.

## Must-know facts
- Normal urine (handout): straw-colored, aromatic, clear or slightly turbid, pH 4.5-8, specific gravity 1.010-1.020, no white cells, red cells, albumin or E. coli, few mucus threads.
- Urinary tract infection: urine culture positive for E. coli, white cells (pyuria) and sometimes blood.
- Stones: blood in urine, pus cells, crystals; the stone itself is analyzed.
- Acute glomerulonephritis: hematuria, proteinuria, casts; high BUN and creatinine, high potassium, low sodium; positive antibody test for streptococcus.
- Nephrotic syndrome: massive proteinuria, some white cells.
- Acute renal failure: azotemia, high potassium and phosphate, low calcium, acidosis, casts, proteinuria.
- Chronic kidney failure: waste retention (uremia), hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, dilutional hyponatremia, high magnesium, anemia, low platelets.
- Fluid volume deficit: high specific gravity, urine osmolality above about 450, BUN raised out of proportion to creatinine, high hematocrit, low urine sodium and chloride.
- Fluid volume excess: dilute urine (low specific gravity), low BUN and hematocrit (dilution), higher urine sodium as the kidney tries to excrete the extra fluid.
- Serum osmolality 285-295; falls in overload and rises in dehydration. Urine osmolality 50-1200. Hematocrit about 39-49% in men and 35-45% in women.

## Assessment
Compare results with the client's baseline. A single value is less useful than the trend.

## Priority nursing actions
- Report critical values (high potassium, very low sodium) to the physician promptly.
- Collect clean-catch urine for culture before antibiotics.
- Trend daily weight and urine specific gravity.

## How the exam asks about it
A urine specific gravity of 1.030 with high hematocrit = dehydration. Protein plus red cells plus casts = glomerular injury.

## How to reason about it
Concentrated blood = dehydrated; diluted blood = overloaded. Leaky filter = protein in urine; inflamed filter = blood and protein.

## Related topics
[[Urine Volume Control and Normal Urine Values]], [[Electrolyte Normal Values and Fluid Balance Lab Tests]], [[Acute Renal Failure: Causes, Phases and Findings]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout gives no values for BUN or creatinine; look up reference ranges in your laboratory text.

title: Fluid Balance Monitoring: Weight, Intake and Output, Edema
body:
## What it is
Nurses detect fluid trouble early by watching a small set of simple measurements: weight, intake and output, edema, neck veins, lung sounds, skin and tongue turgor and urine concentration.

## Must-know facts
- Daily weight is the most reliable simple sign of fluid gain or loss: a gain of about 1 kg (2.2 lb) equals roughly 1 L of retained fluid.
- Intake and output: at least every 8 hours in fluid deficit; hourly in major burns, where urine output of 30-50 mL/hr is the target.
- Pitting edema is graded on a scale from 1 (minimal) to 4 (severe); limb swelling can be tracked by measuring circumference with a tape.
- Fluid deficit: poor skin and tongue turgor, flat neck veins, fast weak pulse, low blood pressure on standing, concentrated urine. Fluid excess: distended neck veins, crackles, edema, high blood pressure and pulse pressure.
- Urine specific gravity rises in dehydration and falls in overload.
- Infants have a larger share of body water (about 80%) and older adults have a weaker thirst sense, so both groups dehydrate quickly.

## Assessment
Weigh at the same time, on the same scale, in similar clothing. Check lung sounds regularly in at-risk clients. Compare skin turgor on the forehead or sternum in older adults.

## Priority nursing actions
- Airway and breathing first if crackles, breathlessness or orthopnea appear: sit the client upright in semi-Fowler's.
- Report rapid weight changes, little urine, or new edema.
- In fluid deficit: replace fluids as ordered, offer small amounts of oral rehydration solution, give mouth care, treat nausea.
- In fluid excess: restrict sodium, avoid over-the-counter drugs containing sodium, reposition often to protect edematous skin, allow rest.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
Isotonic solutions for low blood pressure, half-strength saline later for water; diuretics for overload.

## Complications and red flags
Hypovolemic shock, pulmonary edema, electrolyte disturbance, pressure injury of swollen tissue.

## Client teaching
Weigh daily, read food labels for salt, and report sudden weight gain, swelling or breathlessness.

## How the exam asks about it
"Which finding best shows fluid is accumulating?" Weight gain. "Which finding best shows dehydration?" Concentrated urine with weight loss.

## How to reason about it
Body weight changes faster than anything else when water is gained or lost, and one liter weighs about a kilogram.

## Related topics
[[Fluid Volume Deficit (Hypovolemia)]], [[Fluid Volume Excess (Hypervolemia)]], [[Body Fluid Compartments and Fluid Movement]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout oral rehydration brand names are not repeated; use your facility's products. Hourly urine targets outside burns come from your textbook.

title: Reading an Arterial Blood Gas Step by Step
body:
## What it is
A repeatable way to read any blood gas: first the pH, then the cause, then the body's attempt to compensate.

## Must-know facts
- Normal values from the handout: pH 7.35-7.45; PCO2 35-45 mmHg; PO2 80-100 mmHg; bicarbonate 22-26.
- pH below 7.35 means acidosis; above 7.45 means alkalosis.
- PCO2 reflects breathing: high PCO2 with low pH = respiratory acidosis (too little ventilation); low PCO2 with high pH = respiratory alkalosis (hyperventilation).
- Bicarbonate reflects the metabolic side: low bicarbonate with low pH = metabolic acidosis; high bicarbonate with high pH = metabolic alkalosis.
- Typical causes: respiratory acidosis from aspiration, atelectasis, pneumothorax, sedatives, sleep apnea, ARDS, weak muscles (muscular dystrophy, myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barre); respiratory alkalosis from anxiety and sepsis; metabolic acidosis from DKA, kidney failure, diarrhea, starvation, lactic acidosis; metabolic alkalosis from vomiting, NG suction, antacids, thiazide diuretics.

## Assessment
- Respiratory acidosis: fast pulse and breathing, head fullness, PaCO2 above 60 is severe.
- Respiratory alkalosis: light-headedness, tingling, low potassium.
- Metabolic acidosis: deep rapid breathing, lethargy, hypotension, high potassium.
- Metabolic alkalosis: weakness, cramps, twitching, low potassium and chloride.

## Priority nursing actions
- Step 1: pH. Step 2: PCO2 (respiratory?) and bicarbonate (metabolic?). Step 3: decide which one explains the pH. Step 4: if the other value has moved the opposite way to restore the pH, the body is compensating.
- Treat the cause: ventilate for respiratory acidosis (airway first), calm and slow breathing for anxiety, fluids and insulin for DKA, chloride and potassium for alkalosis with low chloride.
- Re-check ABGs and electrolytes after treatment.

## Treatment and medications (general terms)
Oxygen as ordered, bicarbonate for low bicarbonate, KCl for alkalosis with low potassium, dialysis for severe metabolic acidosis.

## Complications and red flags
Dysrhythmias, falling consciousness, tetany in alkalosis, respiratory failure.

## How the exam asks about it
Given three numbers, name the disorder; then choose the first action (usually airway and breathing).

## Memory aid
"ROME": Respiratory Opposite (pH and PCO2 move in opposite directions), Metabolic Equal (pH and bicarbonate move the same way).

## How to reason about it
The cause is the value that matches the pH direction. The trap: a normal pH with abnormal PCO2 and bicarbonate means full compensation, not a normal client.

## Related topics
[[Arterial Blood Gas Basics]], [[Metabolic Acidosis]], [[Respiratory Acidosis]]

## Check against your textbook
Compensation rules and the partial versus full compensation terms are not in the handout; confirm them in your textbook.
